conflicts/boxer-rebellion/name: The Boxer Uprising and the Allied intervention
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/religionRoleNo: Hostility to Christianity was at the heart of the Boxer movement: its placards blamed missionaries and converts for drought and disorder, and Chinese Christians were by far its most numerous victims. Yet historians such as Joseph Esherick and Paul Cohen stress that the anti-Christian violence grew out of a wider crisis — foreign imperial pressure, the legal privileges missionaries won for converts, village feuds, and a catastrophic drought in north China — and that the Qing court backed the Boxers for dynastic and anti-foreign rather than religious reasons. On the Allied side religion was not a war aim, though missionaries supplied grievances, guides and indemnity claims, and some Western rhetoric framed the relief of the legations as the rescue of Christian civilisation. Religion is therefore best described as a major, not the sole, driver.

conflicts/boxer-rebellion/sides/0/faith: Chinese popular religion: spirit-possession martial arts, Daoist and Buddhist deities, heroes of popular opera

conflicts/boxer-rebellion/summary: A popular movement of north Chinese villagers, the Boxers, attacked missionaries and above all Chinese Christian converts in 1899–1900, blaming them for drought and foreign encroachment. When the Qing court declared war on the foreign powers in June 1900, the Beijing legations and the Catholic Beitang cathedral were besieged until an eight-nation army relieved them in August; Allied punitive expeditions and looting followed, and the 1901 Boxer Protocol imposed a vast indemnity on China. Some 30,000 Chinese Catholics, around 2,000 Chinese Protestants and roughly 200 foreign missionaries and their children were killed.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/story:
By the 1890s Christianity in China was entangled with foreign power. The ‘unequal treaties’ after the Opium Wars and the Tianjin and Beijing conventions of 1858–60 protected missionaries and allowed them to buy property in the interior; France claimed a protectorate over Catholic missions, and missionaries frequently intervened with magistrates on behalf of converts in lawsuits. To many villagers, converts appeared to be a privileged community that refused to contribute to temple festivals and could call on foreign gunboats. ‘Missionary cases’ (jiao’an) — riots, disputed property and lawsuits — multiplied, especially in Shandong. When two German Catholic missionaries were murdered at Juye in November 1897, Germany used the incident to seize Jiaozhou Bay, deepening the identification of mission with conquest.

The Boxers emerged in western Shandong in 1898–99 among poor peasants hit by Yellow River floods and then a severe drought. They practised martial-arts rituals in which young men were possessed by gods drawn from popular novels and opera and believed themselves invulnerable to bullets; girls’ groups, the Red Lanterns, claimed comparable powers. Their placards declared that rain would not fall until the foreigners and their ‘secondary devils’ — the converts — were destroyed, and their slogan became ‘Support the Qing, destroy the foreign’ (fu Qing mie yang). The killing of the English missionary Sidney Brooks on 31 December 1899 was the first death of a foreign missionary, but from the start most of those killed were Chinese Christians.

In spring 1900 the movement spread across the drought-stricken plains of Zhili towards Beijing and Tianjin, burning churches, railway stations and telegraph lines. Factions at court, led by Prince Duan and supported by the Empress Dowager Cixi, saw the Boxers as a loyal militia against foreign aggression. A first relief column under the British admiral Edward Seymour was turned back in mid-June; the Allies stormed the Dagu (Taku) forts on 17 June; on 20 June the German minister Clemens von Ketteler was shot in the street, and on 21 June the court declared war on the foreign powers. For fifty-five days some 900 foreigners and around 3,000 Chinese Christians held out in the Legation Quarter, while about 3,400 Catholics, with French and Italian marines, defended the Beitang (Northern) cathedral under Bishop Alphonse Favier.

The worst massacres took place in the provinces. At Baoding at the end of June and start of July American Presbyterian and Congregational missionaries were killed; at Taiyuan on 9 July the governor of Shanxi, Yuxian, had some forty-four foreign Protestants and Catholics, including women and children, executed in his yamen, and many more Chinese Christians were killed across Shanxi, Zhili and Inner Mongolia. Some converts renounced their faith to save their lives; many were killed in whole families. Southern governors-general, notably Li Hongzhang, Zhang Zhidong and Liu Kunyi, ignored the declaration of war and protected foreigners in the ‘Mutual Protection of the Southeast’, limiting the war to the north.

A second, larger Allied army of about 20,000 men marched from Tianjin in early August and relieved the legations on 14 August; Cixi and the emperor fled to Xi’an. What followed was itself an atrocity: Beijing was systematically looted, by soldiers, diplomats and some missionaries, and German-led punitive expeditions under Field Marshal von Waldersee burned villages suspected of Boxer sympathy and executed suspects with little or no trial. Kaiser Wilhelm II had told his departing troops at Bremerhaven on 27 July to give no quarter and make the name of Germany feared ‘like the Huns’. On the Amur, Russian forces drove thousands of Chinese residents of Blagoveshchensk into the river to drown in July 1900, and Russia occupied Manchuria.

The Boxer Protocol of 7 September 1901 ordered the execution or suicide of senior officials, including Yuxian, permanent foreign garrisons in the capital and an indemnity of 450 million taels payable over thirty-nine years. Missions also negotiated local compensation for destroyed property and murdered converts, sometimes extracting fines from whole villages. The American Board missionary William Scott Ament’s collection of such indemnities was publicly attacked by Mark Twain in ‘To the Person Sitting in Darkness’ (1901), while Hudson Taylor’s China Inland Mission declined compensation for its own losses.

The aftermath reshaped both China and the missions. The Qing undertook late reforms but fell in 1911; Chinese nationalists of the 1920s, in the anti-Christian movement, recalled 1900 as proof that Christianity was the vanguard of imperialism, while churches commemorated the dead as martyrs. Missions grew rapidly in the following decades, and part of the American share of the indemnity was remitted from 1908 to fund Chinese students, leading to Tsinghua University. In 2000 Pope John Paul II canonised 120 Martyrs of China, among them many Catholics killed in 1900 — a canonisation, held on 1 October, China’s National Day, that the People’s Republic denounced as a glorification of imperialism.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/nameOfGod: On the Boxer side the divine was invoked through popular religion: possessing deities such as Guan Yu and the Monkey King, charms and incantations that promised invulnerability, and placards announcing that heaven withheld rain because of the foreign religion. On the Christian side, missionaries and converts interpreted the killings as martyrdom and the defence of the Beitang as divine deliverance; Western propaganda and some sermons cast the relief of the legations as the defence of Christian civilisation against heathen barbarism, and missionaries such as Ament defended punitive indemnities as just retribution.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/religiousCause: Boxer ideology blamed the Christian religion for offending the gods, causing the drought and disrupting village harmony, and its placards called for killing missionaries and converts.
Converts’ refusal to contribute to temple festivals and opera performances made them appear as dissenters from village religious life.
Missionary intervention in lawsuits on behalf of converts, and French claims to protect Catholics, created resentment of Christians as a protected caste.
Rumours about missions — that orphanages killed children for their eyes and hearts, and that churches practised sorcery — were spread in anti-Christian tracts since the 1860s.
Disputes over church property, including the return of old Catholic sites under the 1860 Beijing Convention, turned temples and land into flashpoints.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/otherCauses/0: The ‘scramble for concessions’ of 1897–98, including the German seizure of Jiaozhou Bay and Russian, British and French leases, created fear that China would be partitioned.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/otherCauses/1: Yellow River floods in 1898 and severe drought in 1899–1900 left young men idle and hungry across Shandong and Zhili.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/otherCauses/2: Railways, telegraphs and imported goods disrupted the carting, boat and handicraft trades on which many depended.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/otherCauses/3: Court politics after the failed Hundred Days’ Reform of 1898 strengthened conservative, anti-foreign princes around Cixi.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/otherCauses/4: A tradition of martial-arts societies and anti-dynastic sects in north China supplied networks and rituals.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/triggers/0: The murder of two German Catholic missionaries at Juye in November 1897 and Germany’s seizure of Jiaozhou Bay in response.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/triggers/1: The spread of Boxer bands from Shandong into Zhili in spring 1900 during drought.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/triggers/2: The Allied attack on the Dagu forts on 17 June 1900 and the shooting of the German minister von Ketteler on 20 June.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/triggers/3: The Qing court’s declaration of war on the foreign powers on 21 June 1900.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/timeline/0/tex: Two German missionaries of the Society of the Divine Word are killed at Juye, Shandong; Germany seizes Jiaozhou Bay.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/timeline/1/tex: Yellow River floods devastate Shandong; the Hundred Days’ Reform ends in Cixi’s coup.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/timeline/2/tex: Boxer groups clash with converts in north-west Shandong; the Anglican missionary Sidney Brooks is killed on 31 December.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/timeline/3/tex: June: Boxers enter Beijing and Tianjin; the Seymour expedition is turned back; the Dagu forts fall; von Ketteler is killed; the court declares war (21 June).
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/timeline/4/tex: June–August: siege of the Legation Quarter and the Beitang cathedral; massacres of missionaries and converts at Baoding and Taiyuan (9 July).
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/timeline/5/tex: July: Russian forces drown thousands of Chinese at Blagoveshchensk; Wilhelm II’s ‘Hun speech’ at Bremerhaven (27 July).
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/timeline/6/tex: 14 August: the eight-nation relief force enters Beijing; Cixi flees to Xi’an; looting and punitive expeditions follow.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/timeline/7/tex: 7 September: the Boxer Protocol imposes an indemnity of 450 million taels and executions of officials.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/timeline/8/tex: Shanxi University is founded with Shanxi indemnity funds at Timothy Richard’s proposal; Cixi returns to Beijing.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/timeline/9/tex: The United States begins remitting part of its indemnity to fund Chinese students.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/timeline/10/te: Pope John Paul II canonises 120 Martyrs of China, many of them killed in 1900.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/keyPeople/0/ro: Effective ruler of the Qing dynasty
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/keyPeople/0/fo: Allowed the Boxers into the capital and sanctioned the declaration of war on the powers in June 1900, then fled to Xi’an.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/keyPeople/0/ou: Returned in 1902, blamed subordinates, and presided over the late Qing reforms until her death in 1908.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/keyPeople/1/ro: Governor of Shandong, then of Shanxi
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/keyPeople/1/fo: Patronised the Boxers and ordered the execution of foreign missionaries and their families at Taiyuan on 9 July 1900.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/keyPeople/1/ou: Executed in 1901 at the Allies’ demand under the Boxer Protocol.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/keyPeople/2/fo: Directed the defence of the Beitang cathedral, where thousands of Chinese Catholics endured a two-month siege.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/keyPeople/2/ou: Survived; later criticised for his part in post-war reprisals and compensation claims.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/keyPeople/3/ro: Founder of the China Inland Mission
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/keyPeople/3/fo: His mission lost more members than any other — 58 adults and 21 children; he directed that no compensation be demanded.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/keyPeople/3/ou: The refusal was widely noted in China; he retired soon afterwards and died at Changsha in 1905.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/keyPeople/4/fo: Negotiated a Shanxi settlement in which indemnity money funded a modern university rather than punishment.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/keyPeople/4/ou: Shanxi University opened in 1902; he is remembered as a reformist voice within missions.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/keyPeople/5/fo: Led armed parties collecting indemnities and goods from villages for murdered converts after the relief.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/keyPeople/5/ou: Satirised by Mark Twain in 1901, he became a symbol of missionary complicity in reprisals.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/keyPeople/6/fo: Arrived after the relief and directed dozens of punitive expeditions into the countryside in 1900–01.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/keyPeople/6/ou: Returned to Germany in 1901; the expeditions became notorious for summary executions.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/keyPeople/7/fo: Kept south China out of the war and negotiated the Boxer Protocol.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/keyPeople/7/ou: Died in November 1901, weeks after signing it.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/casualties/not: The best-documented figures concern Christians: roughly 30,000 Chinese Catholics and about 2,000 Chinese Protestants were killed, together with some 200 foreign missionaries and their children (about 136 Protestant adults and 53 children, and over 40 Catholic priests, brothers and sisters). Allied military deaths were about 2,500. The number of Boxers, Qing soldiers and Chinese civilians killed in fighting, at Blagoveshchensk and in Allied punitive expeditions was never counted; total estimates of 100,000 or more are common but rest on little systematic evidence.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/effects/0: The Boxer Protocol of 1901 burdened the Qing with a 450-million-tael indemnity and foreign garrisons, hastening the dynasty’s collapse in 1911.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/effects/1: Russia occupied Manchuria, a step towards the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–05.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/effects/2: The court turned to the New Policies reforms, including the abolition of the civil-service examinations in 1905.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/effects/3: The episode fixed in Western culture the image of the ‘Yellow Peril’, and in Chinese nationalism the image of imperialist looting and humiliation.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/effects/4: Remitted American and British indemnity funds paid for Chinese students abroad and institutions such as Tsinghua University.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/effectsOnChurc: Catholic and Protestant churches commemorated thousands of martyrs; the 2000 canonisation of the Martyrs of China made 1900 central to Catholic memory and sharpened tension with Beijing.
Missions expanded rapidly after 1901, with more schools, hospitals and universities, partly as a deliberate response to the uprising.
Missionary participation in looting and indemnity collection discredited missions in Chinese eyes and fed the 1920s anti-Christian movement.
Some missionaries and Chinese Christian leaders drew the lesson that churches must be self-governing and detached from foreign power, a theme later taken up in indigenous and Three-Self movements.
Local Christian communities, especially in Shanxi and Zhili, were left with enduring divisions between families who had apostatised and those who had suffered.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/legacy: The Boxer Uprising remains contested in memory. For decades after 1949 Chinese historiography celebrated it as patriotic anti-imperialism; since the 1980s scholars have also stressed its superstition and cruelty towards fellow Chinese. For the churches it is both a story of martyrdom and an uncomfortable example of how closely mission had become bound to gunboats, treaties and indemnities.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/dissenters/0/n: James Hudson Taylor and the China Inland Mission
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/dissenters/0/t: Although the CIM suffered the heaviest losses, Taylor and the mission refused to claim indemnity for their own losses, arguing that Christians should not exact payment for suffering endured for Christ.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/dissenters/1/t: The Welsh Baptist argued against punitive fines and proposed instead that Shanxi’s indemnity fund a modern university to educate Chinese students.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/dissenters/2/n: Critics of the looting within the missionary and church press
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/dissenters/2/t: Several missionaries and church newspapers in Britain and the United States condemned the participation of missionaries in looting and punitive raids as a betrayal of the gospel.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/campaigns/0/pe: About 2,000 sailors and marines of eight nations under Admiral Edward Seymour
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/campaigns/0/te: Setting out by rail on 10 June 1900 to relieve the legations, the column was blocked by Boxers and Qing troops near Langfang, retreated along the Hai River and was itself rescued at the Xigu Arsenal on 25 June.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/campaigns/1/ti: The relief of the Beijing legations
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/campaigns/1/pe: About 20,000 Japanese, Russian, British, American and French troops; British commander Alfred Gaselee
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/campaigns/1/te: Leaving Tianjin on 4 August, the allied army defeated Qing forces at Beicang and Yangcun, reached Tongzhou on 12 August and broke into Beijing on 14 August; the Beitang was relieved two days later.
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/campaigns/2/ti: The flight of the court to Xi’an
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/campaigns/2/pe: Empress Dowager Cixi, the Guangxu Emperor and the court
conflicts/boxer-rebellion/campaigns/2/te: Disguised as commoners, Cixi and the emperor left Beijing on 15 August 1900 and travelled through Shanxi to Xi’an, returning in January 1902 after the Protocol was signed.
